Dear Thomas,

You may remember my triumphant note last week saying that focus blocks cut my evening emails by an hour a day. I did not sleep well on it. Three good days could just be a quiet week. So I carried on for four weeks and made week three a normal week without focus blocks, to compare. The result is less exciting: with the blocks I cleared my inbox about twenty minutes earlier each day, not an hour. But the plain week was clearly slower, so the gain is real, only smaller. I am still using the blocks and I have told the team the smaller number. Thank you for asking me how I knew.

Zainab

Jyoti, you asked why I don't trust quick results anymore. Here's Rajni's story from the clinic last year.
I ran the reception desk, and I tried a new appointment reminder, an SMS the evening before. In the first week, missed appointments dropped from twelve to five. I was ready to tell the whole chain.
Then I thought, what if it was just a quiet week? Monsoon had started. Maybe fewer people were travelling anyway.
So I kept going for four more weeks. And for comparison, I looked at the same four weeks from last year, and I also switched the reminders off for one week in the middle to see what happened.
The real drop was smaller than I'd thought. Not twelve to five. More like twelve to nine. But it held every week, and it came back up when I switched the reminders off.
Smaller, but real. That's what I reported.

qa.q: How many missed appointments were there in the first week with reminders?
qa.a: In the first week, missed appointments dropped from twelve to five.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel after the first week?
qa.a: Rajni felt excited and ready to tell the whole chain, before doubting the result.

qa.q: Why was switching reminders off for one week a useful step?
qa.a: It showed that missed appointments came back up without reminders, so the drop was really because of them.

qa.q: How might the clinic chain see Rajni's report?
qa.a: They may trust it more because it is honest about a smaller effect and backed by several weeks of checks.

grounding: It shows a clinic receptionist doubting an early result, extending the trial for four weeks with a comparison period, and finding the gain smaller than it first looked but still real.

I'm Parveen, and I share a desk with Sangeeta at the school's admin office. In June she started a small experiment and I watched it grow.
She tried sending parents a short weekly summary instead of daily notices, hoping fewer would call the office with questions. In the first week, calls dropped from about forty to twenty. She was thrilled, and I thought that was that.
But the next morning she frowned at her notes and said, "It was exam week. Parents were busy." So she kept going. Four more weeks of weekly summaries. And she dug out the call register from the same month last year to compare. She even went back to daily notices for one week, on purpose.
At the end she showed me the chart. Calls went down by about eight a week, not twenty. Smaller than she'd hoped, but it stayed down every week.
I think she was a little disappointed. But she looked sure.

qa.q: How many calls came in the first week of weekly summaries?
qa.a: In the first week, calls dropped from about forty to twenty.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta frowning at her notes the next morning suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt doubtful and uneasy about the first result, suspecting exam week had made it look too good.

qa.q: Why was going back to daily notices for one week useful?
qa.a: It gave a comparison, showing whether calls rose again without the summaries, so the real effect could be seen.

qa.q: How might Parveen see the final chart?
qa.a: Parveen sees a smaller but steady drop and thinks Sangeeta looked a little disappointed but sure.

grounding: It shows a woman doubting an early drop in calls, extending the trial for four weeks with a comparison period, and finding a smaller but real gain.
